source_text: Deinde post dies paucos Pudens miles optio, praepositus carceris, nos magnificare coepit intellegens magnam uirtutem esse in nobis; qui multos ad nos admittebat, ut et nos et illi inuicem refrigeraremus. Ut autem proximauit dies muneris, intrat ad me pater meus consumptus taedio, et coepit barbam suam euellere et in terram mittere, et prosternere se in faciem, et inproperare annis suis et dicere tanta uerba quae mouerent uniuersam creaturam. Ego dolebam pro infelici senecta eius.
thought_title: The jailer shows honor and my father pleads in grief
orientation: Perpetua is still writing her own prison diary after her vision about Dinocrates, now as the day of execution draws near.
pass_a_gloss: Then after a few days Pudens, soldier attendant, overseer of the prison, began to hold us in high honor, understanding that great power was in us; who was letting in many to us, in order that both we and they might give relief to each other in turn. But when the day of the public games drew near, my father enters to me worn out with grief, and he began to tear out his beard and to throw it to the ground, and to throw himself down on his face, and to reproach his years and to speak such great words as would move the whole creation. I was grieving for his unhappy old age.

lemmas.gloss: to hold in high honor here
power at work in them here
public games where sentence is carried out

choices.english: began to hold us in high honor
choices.why: magnificare here is esteem shown by favors, not praise in words
virtus in martyrdom context is operative power perceived by outsider, not moral virtue

choices.english: might give relief to each other in turn
choices.why: brief glossary fixes refrigerare as relief, and inuicem makes it mutual
brief glossary fixes munus as imperial birthday beast and gladiatorial show

pass_b_english: A few days later Pudens, the soldier who served as assistant officer in charge of the prison, began to hold us in high honor, for he understood that great power was at work in us. He let many visitors in to see us, so that we and they might give relief to each other in turn.

As the day of the public games drew near, my father came in to me worn out with grief. He began tearing out his beard and throwing it to the ground. He threw himself facedown. He reproached his own years and spoke words that would have moved the whole of creation. I grieved for his unhappy old age.
